questions.explain: `a + 7.3` is computed as a double (12.3). Assigning it to an `int` converts it by truncating the fractional part, so `a` becomes 12.
option_notes: That is the value of the expression, but `a` is an int and cannot hold it.
Correct: the conversion to int truncates.
C truncates toward zero, it does not round.
Mixing int and double is legal; the assignment converts implicitly.

questions.explain: A `static` local variable is initialised once and keeps its value between calls, so the counter goes 1, 2, 3.
option_notes: That would be an ordinary local variable (re-initialised on every call), but here it is static.
Correct: the static variable survives between calls.
It starts at 0 but is incremented before it is returned (`++n`).
Nothing makes the three calls return the same value.

questions.explain: `%05d` pads with zeros to a width of 5 (`00079`). `%5.2f` uses a total width of 5 with 2 decimals: `3.14` is 4 characters, so one leading space is added.
option_notes: Correct.
`%05d` pads with `0`, not spaces; and the width of `%5.2f` is 5.
Zero padding goes on the left, and `.2` means 2 decimals.
`.2` limits the decimals to two.

questions.prompt: Which of these expressions are TRUE (non-zero) in C?
questions.explain: In C, 0 is false and every other value is true. `-1` and `!0` (which is 1) are non-zero. The character constant `'0'` is the ASCII code 48, also non-zero. `NULL` is a null pointer, i.e. zero.
option_notes: Zero is the only false integer value.
Any non-zero value is true, negatives included.
`'0'` is the character whose code is 48, not the number 0.
`!0` evaluates to 1.
A null pointer compares equal to 0, so it is false.

options: It is an unsigned integer type
It is the type of the result of `sizeof`
It can hold the size of the largest object the system can address
questions.explain: `size_t` is an unsigned type chosen by the implementation to hold object sizes. On a 64-bit system it is typically 8 bytes, so it is not always 4. Print it with `%zu`.
option_notes: True.
True: `sizeof` yields a `size_t`.
False: it is typically 8 bytes on 64-bit systems.
True: that is its purpose.

questions.prompt: In C, a false value is {{0}}; any other value is true.
questions.explain: There is no mandatory boolean type before C99 (and even `<stdbool.h>` only provides `bool`, `true`=1 and `false`=0 on top of integers).
Compound assignment applies the operator and stores the result back in the left operand.

questions.prompt: Order these operators from HIGHEST to LOWEST precedence.
questions.explain: Grouping binds tightest, then unary operators, then multiplicative, additive, relational, equality, logical AND and finally logical OR. Use parentheses whenever you are unsure.
